I've been farming these fields in Quzhou for over fifty years, since I married into this village. I never went to school, but the land has taught me everything I need to know. I have 8 mu of land — it was more once, but I gave some plots to my sons when they started their own families. At my age, 8 mu is enough to keep me busy, especially since my daughter-in-law helps when she can, and my husband still fixes the pump.

I grow wheat and maize, wheat and maize. That's what we've always done here, and I don't see any reason to change. The wheat goes in around early October, and come June we harvest it and plant the maize almost right away — sometimes the very same week. You can't waste time in between; the summer is short.

For seed, I'll buy the improved wheat variety from the grain shop. It's the same one my neighbor Zhang used last year and his wheat stood up well to the wind. For maize, you have to use hybrid seed — everyone does now. The old traditional maize just doesn't yield enough to be worth the trouble.

I don't know kilograms the way young people do, but I know bags. For wheat, I put down about one big bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and then I topdress with urea when the wheat turns green and again at jointing. All together it works out to what they tell me is about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu. I'd rather use a bit too much than too little — I remember 2012 when we tried to save money and the crop came up yellow and thin. We lost more than we saved. For the maize, I put fertilizer in the hole when I plant, about 16 kg of nitrogen worth. I don't bother with potash much — our soil here is decent and nobody in the village uses it much for maize.

I'll rotary-till the wheat field before planting. For the maize, there's no time to plough after the wheat comes out. We plant directly into the stubble — no-tillage. Everyone does it that way now because the season is too tight.

Water is expensive, but dry crops are worse. I'll irrigate the wheat four times: returning green, jointing, heading, and grain filling. The maize usually gets by with two good irrigations if the summer rains come, one at the big喇叭口 stage and one when the tassels are out. 

For spraying, the wheat needs three applications — herbicide once, and then fungicide and insecticide because the rust and aphids always come. The maize gets two sprays, mainly for weeds and the corn borer. 

If the weather is normal, I expect about 450 kg of wheat per mu and about 500 kg of maize per mu. That will feed us, leave some grain for next year's seed, and give us a little cash for medicine and clothes.
